overview: This guide explores the Prometheus AI Engineer, a cloud-native coding agent designed to generate and deploy microservices using AWS infrastructure. We cover the setup of AWS Bedrock and Lambda environments, the automated generation of code and CI pipelines, and the deployment process, contrasting this approach with local runners like Ollama 0.9.
key_takeaways: Prometheus AI Engineer leverages AWS Bedrock for LLM inference and Lambda for serverless compute, contrasting with Ollama's local execution model.
The agent automates the full microservice lifecycle, including README generation, test suite creation, and CI pipeline configuration.
Deployment is handled natively within the AWS ecosystem, providing integrated monitoring and automatic scaling capabilities.
The system includes built-in cost-optimization features to manage cloud resource usage effectively.
Users must have specific AWS IAM permissions configured for Bedrock and Lambda to utilize the agent's capabilities.
Prometheus supports multiple programming languages, auto-generating scaffolding tailored to the user's choice.
prerequisites: Active AWS Account with Business or Enterprise support tier (recommended for Bedrock access)
AWS CLI installed and configured with valid credentials
IAM User permissions for Amazon Bedrock (InvokeModel) and AWS Lambda (CreateFunction, UpdateFunctionCode)

step_by_step.title: Step 1: Configure AWS Environment for Bedrock and Lambda
step_by_step.description: Before using Prometheus, you must ensure your AWS environment is authenticated and has the necessary services enabled. This involves setting up the AWS CLI with a profile that has permissions to access Amazon Bedrock models and create Lambda functions. Verify that Bedrock is enabled in your specific region.
step_by_step.code_example:
# Install AWS CLI if not present
# pip install awscli

# Configure credentials
aws configure --profile prometheus-engineer

# Verify Bedrock access (ensure models are enabled in console)
aws bedrock list-foundation-models --region us-east-1 --profile prometheus-engineer

step_by_step.title: Step 2: Generate Microservice Scaffolding
step_by_step.description: Interact with the Prometheus interface to generate your microservice. While the agent handles the 'Press a button' workflow, it outputs a standard project structure including a SAM template (for Lambda), a package.json (for Node.js), or a requirements.txt (for Python). Below is an example of the SAM template structure the agent typically generates to define the infrastructure.
step_by_step.code_example:
# template.yaml (Generated by Prometheus)
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: Auto-generated microservice by Prometheus

Resources:
  MyFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: app.handler
      Runtime: python3.9
      CodeUri: ./src
      Events:
        ApiEvent:
          Type: Api
          Properties:
            Path: /{proxy+}
            Method: ANY

step_by_step.title: Step 3: Deploy and Monitor via AWS Console
step_by_step.description: Once the code is generated, Prometheus triggers the deployment process. You can verify the deployment and monitor the microservice using the AWS CLI or CloudWatch. The agent typically sets up a CloudWatch Log Group automatically. Use the following command to tail the logs of the deployed service.
step_by_step.code_example:
# Deploy the generated stack (if using SAM CLI)
sam deploy --guided

# Monitor logs for the specific function
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/MyFunction --follow --profile prometheus-engineer

pro_tips: Enable Cost Anomaly Detection in AWS Billing Console to work in tandem with Prometheus's cost-optimization suggestions.
Use AWS Bedrock's 'Provisioned Throughput' if your generated microservice requires high consistency and low latency for LLM calls.
Regularly review the IAM policies generated by Prometheus to ensure the principle of least privilege is maintained.
common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Missing Model Access. Users often forget to explicitly request access to specific foundation models (like Claude 3 or Titan) in the AWS Bedrock console, causing the agent to fail during inference.
Pitfall 2: Region Mismatch. Prometheus might default to us-east-1 for Bedrock, but if your Lambda or S3 buckets are in us-west-2, latency and cross-region costs will increase.
Pitfall 3: Timeout Settings. Generated Lambda functions often default to 3-second timeouts, which is insufficient for LLM inference; ensure the agent sets timeouts to at least 30-60 seconds.

faq.question: How does Prometheus AI Engineer differ from using Ollama 0.9?
faq.answer: Prometheus is a cloud-native agent tightly integrated with AWS services like Bedrock and Lambda, designed for enterprise-grade deployment and scalability. Ollama 0.9 focuses on running open-source models locally on your hardware, offering privacy and zero cloud costs but lacking enterprise infrastructure integration.

faq.question: Do I need to write a Dockerfile to use Prometheus?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. While Prometheus can generate containerized deployments, it primarily focuses on serverless architectures using AWS Lambda (Zip deployment), which abstracts the OS layer away from the user.

faq.question: What programming languages does the Prometheus agent support?
faq.answer: The agent is designed to be language-agnostic but commonly generates scaffolding for Node.js, Python, and Go, aligning with AWS Lambda's primary runtimes.
